abstract: Descriptions are given of the system of education, training and qualifications of engineers that existed in Great Britain up to 1939, and — in more detail — the system that exists in 1971. It is explained how international and national matters brought about the changes, and from this It Is deduced that, whereas the form of education provided In Great Britain up to 1939 was decided by the form of society, now education is Itself bringing about changes in all aspects of the nation's life. It Is further explained that education, training and organisation of Industry, business and commerce are closely inter-linked, and the whole spectrum should be considered when changes are being made in any one sector of the nation's activities.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: High rise buildings which are increasingly apparent in all our major cities have set problems in power distribution not hitherto encountered in this country This paper poses the advantages of a Spot Network distribution system, draws comparisons with conventional systems and makes reference to the systems utilised in three current projects. Aspects such as fault levels, location of sub-stations, vertical distribution, emergency standby generation, protection and the selection of distribution equipment are discussed. The paper seeks to promote beneficial discussion which is hoped will ultimately result In the adoption of revised standards and values by designers of distribution systems, supply authorities, regulation forming bodies standards authorities and equipment manufacturers.

abstract: Motorways and their lighting Installations have become a striking feature of the urban scene in all South African cities. The Arterial Roads Network in East London is to be constructed over a period of thirteen years at a total cost exceeding R20 million. The author reports on the lighting of motorways already completed and under construction in East London and reviews the problems encountered with lighting equipment in service in a coastal city with severe climatic and corrosion conditions. Ths conclusions arising from the operating experience underline the need for standard specifications for luminaires, as essential supplements to the SABS Code of Practice for Public Lighting. The paper emphasises that Municipal Electrical Engineers, as user of exterior lighting equipment In coastal conditions, should be able to design. operate and maintain lighting installations in service for the economic life of the motorways.

abstract: The paper describes work done towards the construction of a two dimensional analogue field plotter, where the field to be investigated is modelled in electrically conducting paint on conductive paper, or represented by an electrolytic tank. The detecting head of the device moves along any preselected equipotential in the analogue field, and the lines are reproduced on an X-Y recorder, By repeating the process line by line the entire field can be resolved. The process is semi-automatic, in that a preselected line will be followed automatically, but successive lines are selected manually. The movement of the detecting head is controlled from a mini-computer which has as input error signals from the probes on the head.

abstract: Mr Jack raises the interesting point, that full use should be made of the properties of the polyimide armature winding insulation and states that the film has reversible properties above 200 °C. Increasing the normal maximum permissible temperature of the armature winding to a figure above 200 °C (BS 173 stipulates 185°C for class H insulation) means in effect an increase in the rating of the motor provided the ratings of the field system and commutator can also be increased. As the traction motors of the classes 6E and 6E1 locomotives already develop tractive efforts close to, and in excess of, the adhesion limits (depending on rail conditions), increasing the rating (and with it the hauled loads) means that more wheelslips will be encountered. However, the suggestion of operating a polyimide-insulated armature winding at normal maximum temperature in excess of 200 °C could result in considerable savings in a new design of traction motor. Regarding the class B bonding varnish used with mica in the insulation of the commutator segments, BS 173 stipulates a temperature rise, measured by thermometer, of 90 °C for commutators. Under test (short-time and continuous) the commutator temperature rises of the classes 6E and 6E1 traction motors were of the order of 65 °C. This leaves a fair reserve.
